items.title: 52193_Jay McShann oral history interview
items.q: I used to come into clubs and I'd enjoy coming up and listening to Bus Moten's group... then go down on 12th Street and hear Pete Johnson play the blues and Joe Turner sing the blues.

ctx.x: All of that. And then, not to speak of like when I first came to Kansas City, when I first came to Kansas City, I would go somewhere every night and listen because I would get off about 1:30 at night, and during that time, the joints was going until six, seven, eight, 9:00 in the morning, but the place I was working for, I got off at 1:30. So this give me a chance to make all the clubs, you know, and I used to come into clubs and I'd enjoy coming up and listening to Bus Moten's group, leave there and go hear…
steady rock and roll, steady beat. And Joe singing for 30 minutes. Well, I'd never seen anything like that in my life.

items.title: Jay McShann interviewed by Monk Rowe, Sarasota, Florida, April 12, 1996
items.q: every night the guy that was doing the film, Bruce Ricker, Bruce would send Joe [Turner] home with a fifth of scotch

ctx.x: What was it like doing the films? You did the “Hootie Blues” and —

Well we had a lot of fun. A lot of people came up there and got full of that mess, they’d had a little too much you know? And you’d turn and every night the guy that was doing the film, Bruce Ricker, Bruce would send Joe [Turner] home with a fifth of scotch, and another fifth to wake up on. And he’d give him a slab of ribs — and get him two slabs of ribs. One slab is to eat that night, and if he didn’t finish that he’d wake up during the night and eat the rest of it. And then wake up with a slab. A fifth and a…
And “The Last of the Blue Devils.” That was a great little film.
